scope: Compatibility with older workspace services during explicit personal-key authentication; strict temporary-login fallback, credential ownership and vault isolation, canceled/late authentication, modern persistent-device regression, translated safe status diagnostics, and correction of the actual SCons bundle target selected by an existing owned-process test.

findings.problem: The initial patch rejected an echoed shared key only in explicit authentication. Legacy saved-key restoration could still persist the same key as owned and later revoke it. Exact string comparison also missed equivalent Bearer values with surrounding spaces.
findings.resolution: Both enrollment paths reject canonical shared-key echoes and avoid their revocation, including late responses. Personal-key input is normalized after validation while account passwords remain unchanged. Modern identity tests now cover saved-key echo, late echo and whitespace-equivalent keys; the compatibility suite rejects explicit echoed keys without calling the identity fallback.

findings.problem: New formatted status text was interpolated before translation, and the temporary-login suffix did not exactly match its translation key.
findings.resolution: The session uses the Tianxuan translation domain, translates templates before interpolation, translates the exact suffix separately, and includes the connection-failure fragment in the English catalog.

review_checks: Only a definite HTTP 404 or 405 from device enrollment allows an explicit personal key to use the older identity endpoint. HTTP 401/403, other service failures, transport failure, empty successful credentials and shared-key echoes do not downgrade.

Temporary authentication requires an actual successful identity response with a nonblank string actor ID and an allowed admin/editor/viewer role. The server role is preserved; the client grants no additional authority.

The temporary path returns before any vault load/save/delete or old-device cleanup. It activates with owned=false and no saved digest. Its marker survives sign-out so repeated logout cannot read or delete a different saved login.

Authentication generation, captured origin and identity generation continue to reject canceled/superseded login results, origin changes and late 401 replies from an older session. Only distinguishable independent device credentials may be revoked.

Existing owned-device restoration, same-account reauthentication, conditional vault replacement, migration, restart and logout remain covered by the modern identity suite. Shared credentials are never promoted to owned credentials merely because enrollment returned them.

New status messages contain fixed error categories and safe HTTP status indicators. Raw response bodies and keys are not interpolated. The implementation does not rely on a presumed production HTTP status.

The new loopback compatibility suite uses generated credentials and an isolated randomly named credential service. On macOS only its test helper shares the runner OS credential-store scope; the editor remains isolated. Fixtures remove their own service records in finally blocks and check for credential leakage.

The standard identity runner invokes the new compatibility suite and checks unchanged source/binary fingerprints across both runs. This adds routine coverage without a provider invocation or a new production authentication dependency.

The owned-process test locates the exact ainative/bundle.gen.h CommandNoCache registration rather than assuming it is the first generated-header command. It fails if the target is missing and retains the real source-list, packaged helper and installed helper-resolution assertions.

limitations: No production key was read and no authenticated production-service request was made by this reviewer. The actual HTTP status behind the user login failure has not been established by this review; 404/405 compatibility is proven using controlled loopback services.

The new binary and fixtures establish compatibility behavior, not successful real-user reauthentication against the installed service. Installation, live account acceptance, exact-candidate CI and main delivery remain separate evidence.
The temporary compatibility login is deliberately not persisted. Modern supported services continue to use independent persistent device authorization.
